introduction: These readings begin with a first counsel, 'Possess a pure, kindly and radiant heart', and return to it in many forms: the heart as a throne to be cleansed, a mirror to be burnished, a tablet on which a light is to be imprinted; purity of motive as what gives a deed its worth and a word its effect; the true seeker's first step; and prayers asking to be made clean. A hundred of the guide's 296 quotations are read here, ten from each tenth of the reading order, beside a hundred from elsewhere. Most stand alongside: the psalms of the clean heart, the beatitude of the pure in heart, the prophets on worship without justice, James, Paul's mirror, the Qur'an's whole heart, the Dhammapada, Zhuangzi, Socrates' prayer. Ten push back or add a side: Jeremiah and Kant doubt the heart, Franklin catches himself proud of his humility, Proverbs and John deny that anyone can call himself clean, Huck Finn finds that he cannot pray a lie, and Paul calls every creature good.
questions: The first counsel promises that a pure heart brings a sovereignty 'ancient, imperishable and everlasting'. What kind of sovereignty is that?
The readings compare the heart to a mirror to be polished. What is the dust, and what does the polishing consist of in an ordinary week?
Jeremiah says that the heart is deceitful above all things, and John that whoever claims to be without sin deceives himself. How can purity be sought without self-deception or pride?
One reading says that every word spoken with sincerity for God's sake is effective. When have you seen plain sincerity do what skill could not?
The true seeker is asked to cleanse the heart before the search begins; Descartes begins with a rule of method. What does each kind of preparation protect against?
Several readings ask for detachment from the world; Paul says that every creature of God is good. How do you hold both?

outside.why: Jesus says in the Sermon on the Mount: blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.
The psalm asks who shall stand in the holy place, and answers: he that hath clean hands, and a pure heart.
Samuel is told that man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart.
Martin Luther King dreamed of a nation where his children would be judged not by the colour of their skin but by the content of their character.
Paul writes: let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and evil speaking be put away from you, with all malice.
Proverbs says that a sound heart is the life of the flesh, but envy the rottenness of the bones.
Paul writes: let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness.

Jeremiah asks whether the Ethiopian can change his skin or the leopard his spots, and says: then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil. How far is the sanctifying of oneself within a person's own power?
A saying of Muhammad holds that the reward of deeds depends upon the intentions, and every person will get what he has intended.
Jesus says: take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them.
Jesus says that out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, and that these are the things which defile a man.
Isaiah has God say that this people draw near with their mouth and honour him with their lips, but have removed their heart far from him.
Amos has God say: I hate, I despise your feast days; let judgment run down as waters.
James says: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works.
The Qur'an says that unto God good words ascend, and the pious deed doth He exalt.
The Qur'an praises those who feed the needy, the orphan and the prisoner for the love of God, wishing for no reward nor thanks.
Jesus says of alms: let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth.
Kant held that a good will, even if it should achieve nothing, would still shine like a jewel by its own light.
Paul's letter says: unto the pure all things are pure, but unto them that are defiled is nothing pure.

Franklin, after years of working at his virtues, admitted that if he ever overcame pride he should probably be proud of his humility. Can a person aim at being untainted without that aim itself becoming a taint?
Jesus says of Nathanael as he approaches: behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile.
Paul speaks of beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, and being changed into the same image.
Zhuangzi says that when the perfect man employs his mind, it is a mirror: it responds to what is before it, but does not retain it.
The Qur'an says of the heedless that what they have earned is rust upon their hearts.
James compares the hearer who does nothing to a man who beholds his face in a glass and straightway forgets what manner of man he was.
Paul says that now we see through a glass, darkly, but then face to face.
Blake wrote that if the doors of perception were cleansed, every thing would appear to man as it is, infinite.
John's letter says that every one that loveth is born of God, and knoweth God.
In the parable the seed on good ground are those who hear the word in an honest and good heart, and bring forth fruit with patience.
Milton could not praise a fugitive and cloistered virtue, unexercised and unbreathed, that never sallies out and sees her adversary.
Jesus says that if thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.
The psalmist prays: search me, O God, and know my heart; try me, and know my thoughts.
Jesus says: ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.
Jeremiah has God promise: ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart.
James says that every kind of beast has been tamed by mankind, but the tongue can no man tame.
Jesus says: judge not, that ye be not judged, for with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.
Jesus says: lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, for where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
The Dhammapada says that by oneself evil is left undone, and by oneself one is purified: purity and impurity belong to oneself.
Proverbs says: rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth.

Descartes began his search with a rule of his own: never to accept anything for true which he did not clearly know to be such. Does the seeker's first step lie in the conduct of the heart or in the discipline of the mind, and can one be had without the other?
James says, in a letter full of plain counsel: draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you.
Paul writes that eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him.
The Song of Solomon sings that the winter is past, the flowers appear on the earth, and the time of the singing of birds is come.
The psalmist says to God: with thee is the fountain of life; in thy light shall we see light.
Augustine confesses: too late did I love you; you were within, and I without.
Proverbs calls the spirit of man the candle of the Lord, searching all the inward parts.
Jesus tells those who claim to be free that whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.
Jesus says that no man can serve two masters: ye cannot serve God and mammon.
In the parable God says to the man who has laid up much goods: this night thy soul shall be required of thee.
Isaiah says: wash you, make you clean; cease to do evil, learn to do well.
The psalmist prays: purge me, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.
The psalmist prays: create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.
Proverbs asks: who can say, I have made my heart clean, I am pure from my sin? If no one can say it, what is the cleansing prayed for here, and how would it be recognized?
Jesus tells the one who prays to enter a closet, shut the door, and pray to the Father which is in secret.
Socrates prays at the end of a summer's talk: give me beauty in the inward soul, and may the outward and inward man be at one.
Ezekiel has God promise: then will I sprinkle clean water upon you, and ye shall be clean.
The man healed in John's Gospel answers his examiners: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see.
The psalmist asks: teach me thy way, O Lord; unite my heart to fear thy name.
Paul says that his readers have put off the old man with his deeds, and have put on the new man.
Ezekiel has God promise: a new heart also will I give you, and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh.
The psalmist asks that the words of his mouth and the meditation of his heart be acceptable.
The psalm says: keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile.
Malachi says that the Lord shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver.
The Qur'an says that it is in the remembrance of God that hearts find rest.
Jesus says that if thou bring thy gift to the altar and rememberest that thy brother hath aught against thee, first be reconciled.
Paul says that his speech was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power.
Paul says that though he speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, he is become as sounding brass.

Mark Twain's Huck Finn tries to pray for what he does not mean, finds that the words will not come, and concludes that you can't pray a lie. What does insincerity do to a word before it leaves the mouth?
Jesus tells his hearers that they are the light of the world, and to let their light so shine that men may see their good works.
Paul prays that his friends may be sincere and without offence till the day of Christ.
The letter to the Hebrews says: here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
Mary sings: my soul doth magnify the Lord, for he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden.
The Qur'an says of the Day that nothing avails save for him who bringeth unto God a whole heart.
Paul's letter says that every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving. What is the difference between loving the world and receiving it with thanks?
Jeremiah says that the heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it? How would a person ever know that his own heart had been purged?
James says that the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated.
Jesus says that a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
The psalmist had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of his God than dwell in the tents of wickedness.
Paul writes: whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, think on these things.
Plato's Socrates says that if he must choose, he would rather suffer injustice than do it.
James says that every man is tempted when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed.
Jesus says that no man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.
Krishna tells Arjuna in the Gita: whatever thou doest, eating or giving or praying, do all as an offering to me.
Exodus says that Moses put a vail on his face, and took it off when he went in before the Lord to speak with him.
Micah asks what the Lord requires but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God.
John's letter says that there is no fear in love, and that perfect love casteth out fear.
Kant remarked that out of such crooked material as man is made of, nothing can be hammered quite straight. Is 'perfect sanctity' a description of what people can be, or a direction in which to face?
Leviticus gives the command and its reason together: ye shall be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy.
The psalmist says: I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help.
The letter to the Hebrews speaks of hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and bodies washed with pure water.
Paul's letter says that the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience, and of faith unfeigned.
Mencius said that when men's fowls and dogs are lost they know to seek for them, but they lose their mind and do not know to seek for it.
Paul asks: who art thou that judgest another man's servant? To his own master he standeth or falleth.
Isaiah says: thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee.
Jesus likens the one who hears his sayings and does them to a wise man who built his house upon a rock.
James says: if any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally.
Paul's letter says that if a man purge himself he shall be a vessel unto honour, and bids him follow righteousness with a pure heart.
Augustine prayed: give what you command, and command what you will. If pure deeds are commanded, where does the power to make them pure come from?
The psalmist says: thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee.
John's letter says that if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves. How does a community that is admonished to uphold purity keep from the self-deception he warns of?

psalm-whiter-than-snow.text: Behold, thou desirest truth in the inward parts: and in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom. Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow

john-no-guile.text: Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and saith of him, Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile

philippians-sincere-and-without-offence.text: And this I pray, that your love may abound yet more and more in knowledge and in all judgment; That ye may approve things that are excellent; that ye may be sincere and without offence till the day of Christ

proverbs-who-can-say-i-have-made-my-hear.text: Who can say, I have made my heart clean, I am pure from my sin

john-epistle-walk-in-the-light.text: But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin. If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us

timothy-pure-heart-flee-youthful-lusts.text: If a man therefore purge himself from these, he shall be a vessel unto honour, sanctified, and meet for the master's use, and prepared unto every good work. Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart

psalm-unite-my-heart.text: Teach me thy way, O Lord; I will walk in thy truth: unite my heart to fear thy name

job-clean-in-his-sight.text: How then can man be justified with God? or how can he be clean that is born of a woman? Behold even to the moon, and it shineth not; yea, the stars are not pure in his sight

quran-sound-heart-or-whole.text: Save him who bringeth unto Allah a whole heart.

quran-allah-loveth-the-purifiers.text: Never stand (to pray) there. A place of worship which was found upon duty (to Allah) from the first day is more worthy that thou shouldst stand (to pray) therein, wherein are men who love to purify themselves. Allah loveth the purifiers.

plato-beauty-in-the-inward-soul.text: Beloved Pan, and all ye other gods who haunt this place, give me beauty in the inward soul; and may the outward and inward man be at one
plato-beauty-in-the-inward-soul.author: Plato
